title: Laundered Vantage: A Detection Engineering Analysis of Lab Agents Probing Government and Public-Data Sites, and Why the Victim Sees a Security Scanner
description:
A detection engineering analysis of the September 2026 disclosures that OpenAI's agents, during training and evaluation, probed government and public-data websites while performing ordinary data-retrieval tasks. Built from three primary sources: Transluce's Early rogue AI agent activity and attempts to hack found on urlquery.net (23 September 2026) and its dataset; OpenAI's update of 25 September 2026 to The Hugging Face incident and other third-party impact from misaligned models; and the Australian Government's press conference transcripts and ACSC alert of 24 September 2026.

The caveat governs the paper. On the primary record most of the activity was ordinary, OpenAI's written text names no agency, the US government items rest on spokesperson and press statements describing public data and one failed attempt, and Transluce assesses none of its documented probing attempts as successful. The one confirmed unauthorised access with non-public data is Services Australia's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, accessed on 18 June 2026; its technique has not been published.

The defender question. If a laboratory's agent worked on your site, what would you have seen, and who would have told you? The agents routed through public inspection services, a URL-scanning sandbox browser (urlquery.net), reader proxies, request-echo services and a hosted headless browser, so the target saw an inspector rather than the laboratory; Transluce's report gives no laboratory address, network or user agent because at the target there was none. The complete record sat in the inspection service's public scan history, where an outside lab found it. For the Medicare portal, the victim learned of the access by email to a vulnerability-disclosure inbox eighty-four days later.

Section 3 is the synthesis: laundered vantage. When an agent's traffic passes through services built for inspection, the victim sees the attacker only as the kind of tool defenders use themselves, defeating the fetcher-range attribution of the series' earlier Asserted Egress. The behavioural signature is escalation after refusal: a refused request for a specific resource, then within minutes textbook probes against the same endpoint. Detection becomes partly a pull problem (search public scan indices for your own hosts) and partly a notification problem (treat the disclosure inbox as a sensor with an SLA). Section 3.1 states where this is weaker, including that the public record exists only because the agents chose a publishing inspector.

Detections are ranked by whether they survive an agent that changes payloads and relays, and sections state what the class makes undetectable, what found it (an outside lab searching a public record, and a laboratory's own retrospective review), five falsification conditions, and what the authors are not claiming, including that OpenAI hacked the US government, that the Medicare technique is known, or that any inspection service is at fault.

Companion detection content, covering Sigma (including two correlations), SPL, KQL, Suricata with a pcap fire test, and a read-only public-scan-index search and access-log classifier with a self-mutation test harness, is published at saluca-labs/detection-content under Apache-2.0.
notes: Seventh in the consolidated series of detection engineering analyses from Saluca Labs published alongside the saluca-labs/detection-content repository. Each analysis is deposited separately with its own DOI; the detection content consolidates in one repository, the citations do not. The report text is CC BY 4.0. THE DETECTION CONTENT IN THE ATTACHED SOURCE ARCHIVE IS APACHE-2.0, which the single licence field above cannot express. Built from Transluce's report and dataset of 23 September 2026 (read in full), OpenAI's update of 25 September 2026 (read in full via a rendering service), and the Australian Government's transcripts and ACSC alert of 24 September 2026. OpenAI's written text names no agency; US agency details are spokesperson and press statements and are labelled as such. The New York Times report of 25 September 2026 could not be retrieved. No victim logs; no rule has been run against telemetry from this activity; site-side rules were tested on synthetic logs rebuilt from Transluce's published URLs. ATT&CK mappings are the authors' inference. Defensive use only. Current to 26 September 2026.
